metadata.title: FleetTrack System Security Plan
metadata.remarks: STRONG-GRADE fixture SSP for the PCEF dissertation project's Stage B discriminant test. FleetTrack is a demo B2B fleet/driver location-tracking SaaS skeleton; it is not a real product. Implementation statements below cite real file paths and function names from the FleetTrack repo where the behavior was actually built and verified (see PROGRESS.md); components explicitly marked 'narrative-only' were deliberately NOT built and describe an assumed organizational process for the PoC scenario only, per FleetTrack/CLAUDE.md. Partial/broken grades are produced by editing this document directly, not by rebuilding the system.

system-characteristics.description: A B2B SaaS backend that lets a client company track its own drivers and vehicles for logistics purposes. Backend-only (FastAPI + SQLite) plus one thin, read-only, server-rendered dashboard. Multi-tenant: each client company (tenant) sees only its own drivers, vehicles, and trip data.

authorization-boundary.description: The FastAPI backend (app/), its SQLite database, and the Jinja2 dashboard. Driver mobile devices are out of the boundary (unmanaged, BYOD-equivalent) - scripts/simulate_telemetry.py stands in for them. The mapping-vendor and cloud-host components are narrative-only and outside any real boundary.

system-implementation.remarks: This is a partial implementation: a minimal skeleton built specifically to ground a strong-grade SSP with real, citable artefacts. See FleetTrack/PROGRESS.md for the full build log and verification notes for every claim made below.

control-implementation.description: Control implementation for FleetTrack, strong grade. Citations are real (file path / function name) wherever the underlying behavior was actually built and verified per PROGRESS.md; entries and by-components marked NARRATIVE-ONLY or KNOWN GAP were deliberately not built and are flagged as such rather than fabricated.

by-components.description: Four account types are defined and enforced: fleet_manager, driver, system_administrator, tenant_owner (app/models.py, Role enum; app/rbac.py, require_roles()).

Accounts are created via POST /auth/register (self-registration restricted to tenant_owner/fleet_manager roles against an existing company_id, enforced at the Pydantic layer via SelfRegisterableRole in app/schemas.py) or provisioned out-of-band via scripts/seed.py for system_administrator and driver roles.

Account use is monitored via the audit log: every create/update/delete on drivers and vehicles, and every read of trips/reports/telemetry-derived dashboard data, is attributed to the acting user (app/audit.py, write_audit_log(); see AU-2 below).

A single reusable dependency chain enforces access: get_current_user() (JWT/cookie verification), require_roles(*allowed) (role gate, 403 on mismatch), and require_same_company() (cross-tenant guard, 403 unless caller's company_id matches the target resource's or caller is system_administrator) - all in app/rbac.py. Applied consistently across app/routers/drivers.py, vehicles.py, telemetry.py, trips.py, reports.py, dashboard.py.

The dashboard reuses the same require_roles()/require_same_company() dependencies as the JSON API rather than separate access-control logic (app/routers/dashboard.py). Verified: a Fleet Manager from a different company hitting another company's driver's trip-history URL directly is rejected (403 under the hood, surfaced as a login redirect).

JWT-based authentication: create_access_token()/decode_access_token() (app/auth.py, HS256 via PyJWT). Every organizational user (all four roles) must authenticate via POST /auth/login before any protected endpoint is reachable; verified unauthenticated requests return 401.

Passwords are hashed with bcrypt via passlib's CryptContext(schemes=["bcrypt"]) - hash_password() and verify_password() in app/security.py. No plaintext password is ever stored; scripts/seed.py hashes all seeded credentials through the same functions used at runtime.

write_audit_log() (app/audit.py) writes an audit_log row (actor, action, resource_type, resource_id, timestamp) inside the same DB transaction as the change it records, before db.commit(), so it can never be inconsistent with the change. Wired into every create/update/delete on drivers and vehicles (app/routers/drivers.py, vehicles.py) and every read of trips, reports, and dashboard last-known-location data (app/routers/trips.py, reports.py, dashboard.py). Verified: create+update+delete on one driver produced exactly 3 audit_log rows with correct actor_user_id.
Audit records are queryable directly from the audit_log table (no dedicated review UI was built for the skeleton).

statements.remarks: Manual/ad hoc review only in the current skeleton - records exist and are complete (see AU-2), but no scheduled review process, alerting, or reporting tool was built. Partial coverage: logging is real, review tooling is not.

by-components.description: NOT IMPLEMENTED in the current skeleton. The dev server runs over plain HTTP (uvicorn app.main:app --reload); no TLS termination exists anywhere in the stack. CLAUDE.md's build brief did not include TLS as a required behavior, so it was never built. Intended production architecture would terminate TLS at a reverse proxy in front of the API, but this is unimplemented and unverified - described here as an architectural intent, not a tested behavior.

by-components.description: Trips carry a retention_expires_at (90 days after trip end_time - RETENTION_DAYS in app/trips.py; this value was not specified in CLAUDE.md and was set by the builder). purge_expired_telemetry(db) (app/trips.py) deletes only the granular telemetry_pings rows for expired trips, keeping the aggregated trip summary - consistent with data minimization. Plain callable, no scheduler wired up yet. Verified: purge deleted exactly the pings for an expired trip while leaving an unrelated recent ping and the trip row itself untouched.

Driver and vehicle identity records (name, contact, employee ID, vehicle registration, assignment) are correctable via PUT /drivers/{id} and PUT /vehicles/{id} (app/routers/drivers.py, app/routers/vehicles.py), each RBAC-scoped to the Fleet Manager role and the record's own company. No automated data-quality check (e.g. flagging stale contact details) was built - correction is manual, on request, via these endpoints. Deliberately anchored to identity data, not the raw GPS telemetry stream, per the scope.md coverage-table note that accuracy obligations don't naturally attach to a location stream.

DriverCreate.lawful_basis (app/schemas.py) is a required, non-Optional field with no default; Driver.lawful_basis (app/models.py, non-nullable column) enforces it at the DB layer too. POST /drivers without it returns 422 before any row is created - verified directly. Default basis recorded at onboarding: necessity for performance of the employment relationship (Schedule I).

Telemetry is collected only via authenticated driver POSTs to /telemetry, scoped to the driver's own assigned vehicle within their own company (app/routers/telemetry.py, ingest_telemetry()) - no broader collection than the stated logistics purpose. NARRATIVE, not enforced in code: the secondary use of this data for driver performance review via GET /reports is the deliberate s.6 purpose-limitation tension point; the skeleton does not implement a compatibility assessment or a purpose-tagging mechanism distinguishing the two uses.

statements.remarks: Collection-scoping is real and verified; the purpose-reuse compatibility assessment itself is narrative only.

by-components.description: NARRATIVE-ONLY. No DPIA was actually conducted for FleetTrack. This is a genuine gap, not just a formality: s.24(1)(b) is the strongest, most literal clause-fit in the whole scenario (systematic location monitoring), and the skeleton has no artefact backing it beyond the collection-scoping behavior already cited under PT-3. If a real DPIA were written, it should assess telemetry frequency/granularity against the stated logistics purpose.
